pedagogy.summary: This LANGUAGE topic is the vocabulary of data handling — data, tally, frequency, survey, pictogram, bar chart, axis/axes, scale, label, category, discrete vs continuous, line graph, pie chart — learned by USING the words while collecting, organising and presenting data, not by reciting definitions. The two load-bearing distinctions are frequency (the COUNT) versus tally (the marks) versus category (the group), and discrete (counted, whole-number) versus continuous (measured, any value in between). Teaching should introduce each term at the moment it is needed in a real data activity and lean on contrast pairs, because the meaning of 'continuous' lives in its difference from 'discrete'.
bestPractices: Introduce each term in the act of doing — 'we'll TALLY as we count, and the total is the FREQUENCY' — rather than as a word list
Teach the tricky terms as contrast pairs (discrete vs continuous; tally vs frequency; label vs scale) so meaning sits in the difference
Have children LABEL real charts they build (title, axis labels, scale) and say the terms aloud as they place them
Sort real variables into discrete (number of pets, goals scored) vs continuous (height, time, temperature) with a 'could it be in between?' test
keyRepresentations: A chart the child annotates: title, both axis labels, an even scale, category names
A sorting mat for variables: counted vs measured
Tally chart feeding a frequency table (marks → count)
commonMisconceptions: Confuses discrete and continuous — e.g. thinks height is discrete because it's written as a whole number, or that 'continuous' just means 'a lot of data'
Uses 'frequency' for the category name, or conflates the tally marks with the frequency total
Muddles 'label' and 'scale' — calls the category names the scale, or numbers an axis in uneven steps yet still calls it a scale
Calls every display a 'bar chart' or 'graph', not matching the term to the representation

learn.summary: This is a LANGUAGE topic: the vocabulary of data handling — data, tally, tally chart, frequency, frequency table, survey, pictogram, bar chart, axis/axes, scale, label, category, discrete data, continuous data, line graph, pie chart. The words are learned by USING them while collecting, organising and presenting real data, not by reciting definitions. Two load-bearing distinctions carry the topic: frequency (the COUNT) versus tally (the marks) versus category (the group); and discrete (separate values, usually counted, often whole numbers) versus continuous (measured, can take values in between). Introduce each term at the moment it is needed in a real data activity, and lean on contrast pairs, because the meaning of 'continuous' lives in its contrast with 'discrete'.

activities.title: Label the chart and sort the data
feedback: If 'scale' is placed on the category names: the scale is the row of equal number steps up the axis; the labels say what each axis shows. Move it to the number steps.
If height is tagged 'discrete' because it was written as a whole number: ask 'could someone be 125-and-a-half cm?' — yes, so height is continuous; the written figure is just rounded.
If 'frequency' is placed on a category name: the category is the group; the frequency is the count you end with (shown by how tall each bar is). Separate the two roles.
When a tag lands on the part it truly names, confirm it and ask the child to read the term aloud with what it does.
activities.rationale: Vocabulary used in context is best taught by having the child label real charts and sort real variables with immediate feedback — active use rather than passive recognition. An optional interaction that only accepts a tag on the part it truly names (so 'scale' will not stick to the category row) and an 'in-between?' prompt on the sorter make the distinctions concrete; these are illustrative mechanisms, not required ones.
sourceClaims: The statistics programme requires pupils to interpret and construct pictograms, tally charts, block diagrams, tables, bar charts and (later) line and pie charts, and to interpret discrete and continuous data — fixing the vocabulary pupils must use in context

A picture graph uses one symbol per individual whereas a pictograph uses a symbol for several; displays represent the distribution of a categorical or discrete quantitative variable — grounding the terms category, frequency and display type in use
learnerActions: Finish a half-built bar chart by placing the right term onto each part: the title, each axis label, the scale (the equal number steps up the side), the category names along the bottom, and the frequency (the count shown by the height of each bar on the value axis).
Say each term aloud as you place it — 'this is the scale', 'these are the category names', 'this axis shows the frequency' — so you are wielding the word, not just matching it.
Sort real variables into 'discrete (counted)' or 'continuous (measured)': e.g. 'number of pets', 'goals scored' versus 'how tall', 'time taken', 'temperature'.
For each variable, apply the test: 'Could there be a value in between?' — someone can be 125-and-a-half cm tall (continuous) but cannot have two-and-a-half pets (discrete).
activities.intendedInsight: Data vocabulary is mastered by using it correctly in a real chart and a real sorting task — height is continuous because a value can fall in between, even when it is written as a whole number.

activities.title: Tally to frequency: marks become a count
feedback: If the child calls the marks 'the frequency': the marks are the tally; the frequency is the number you get when you total them.
If the child labels the category column 'frequency': the category names the group; the frequency column holds the counts.
Confirm correct use by asking the child to restate 'tally marks -> total -> frequency' in their own words.
activities.rationale: Separating the roles in a real recording task directly targets the common conflation of tally, frequency and category, teaching the terms through the action of recording data.
sourceClaims: The statistics programme requires pupils to interpret and construct pictograms, tally charts, block diagrams, tables, bar charts and (later) line and pie charts, and to interpret discrete and continuous data — fixing the vocabulary pupils must use in context
learnerActions: Run a quick survey (e.g. favourite fruit) and record responses by making tally marks in a tally chart as each one comes in.

When counting is done, total each row and write the frequency in a frequency table — pointing out that the tally is the marks and the frequency is the final count. Then show the same frequencies as a pictogram, with a key that says what one picture stands for, and say 'this is a pictogram' while you build it.
As you work, answer: 'Which part is the tally and which is the frequency?' and 'Which part is the category?'
activities.intendedInsight: Tally (the marks), frequency (the count) and category (the group) are three different roles; the tally feeds the frequency, they are not the same thing.

activities.title: Contrast-pair glossary (scaffold)
feedback: Prompt the child to generate their own example for each side of a pair (one discrete, one continuous) rather than only reading the given one.
If they only read definitions back, return them to the label-and-sort activity to use the term on a real chart or variable.
activities.rationale: A tap-to-reveal, contrast-pair glossary suits vocabulary by showing discrete beside continuous and tally beside frequency with examples. It is a support for recall and contrast; on its own it is recognition-only and does not require the child to construct correct use, so it should feed into, not replace, the label-and-sort activity.
learnerActions: View 'discrete' and 'continuous' side by side, each with a canonical example and the 'could there be a value in between?' test.
View 'tally' beside 'frequency', and 'label' beside 'scale', comparing what each one does.
Tap or point to parts of a chart to reveal their names, then try to name the next part before revealing it.
activities.intendedInsight: Tricky terms are easier to hold when seen as contrast pairs, because the meaning sits in the difference between the two words.

constraints: Teach each term at the point it is needed inside a real data activity, not as an up-front word list.
Recognition and tap-to-reveal glossary tasks support recall but do not, by themselves, elicit independent construction; pair them with building and labelling a chart and sorting real variables.
The contrast-pair glossary is a scaffold: it displays comparisons but does not require the child to use the term, so confirm mastery through active labelling and sorting with feedback.

Matching, categorisation and fill-the-blank items can check correct use (e.g. a discrete/continuous sort with a 'whole-number-written' trap, a tally-versus-frequency match), but keep them as checks alongside the hands-on build rather than the main teaching.

A real survey/chart with actual categories, an even scale and variables to sort is the core for this LANGUAGE objective; picture-only or definition-reciting versions are weaker for eliciting correct use because the vocabulary is learned by wielding it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy row claimed 'Data vocabulary is not spatial; 3D adds nothing' and that open conversation is a poor fit. These are catalog-fit judgements, not established pedagogical laws: a conversation can support vocabulary use if anchored to a real chart/variable, and 3D is simply not needed here rather than proven worthless. Softened accordingly; spoken discussion while building a chart is useful.
The 'tool only accepts a tag on the part it truly names' behaviour is presented as an optional illustrative interaction, not a mandatory mechanism.

The first activity's 'frequency' tag (referenced in feedback) is present in the learner actions and described as the bar chart's value-axis count, matching the original design; verified coherent on this independent pass.

Diagnostic/assessment content (diagnosticPrompt, probeDeeper, errorPatterns) remains in the assessment fields; only its teaching-relevant substance was mirrored into feedback and no assessment field was altered.
The ASA GAISE source distinguishes 'picture graph' from 'pictograph'; the topic uses 'pictogram'. Kept the claim verbatim as source grounding, not as a child-facing definition.

probeDeeper: Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'could someone be 125-and-a-half centimetres tall? could someone have two-and-a-half pets?' to test the discrete/continuous boundary by use
Ask 'as you fill this in, which part is the tally and which is the frequency?' to check the terms are distinguished in action
Ask 'why do the numbers up the side need equal steps — what do we call that part?' to surface 'scale' used correctly
Ask 'is this a bar chart, a pictogram or a line graph — and how can you tell?' to check terms match representations
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for correct USE in context: naming the title, axis labels, an even scale and the categories; using 'frequency' for the counts and 'tally' for the marks; and identifying number of pets as discrete (counted, whole) and height as continuous (measured, can fall between values), justified by the 'in-between' test.

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses discrete and continuous — calls height discrete because it's recorded as a whole number, or thinks 'continuous' just means 'lots of data'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Apply the 'could there be a value in between?' test — someone can be 125.5 cm but not have 2.5 pets; contrast the pair explicitly
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child tags height 'discrete' citing the written figure, or can't apply the counted-vs-measured distinction

errorPatterns.pattern: Uses 'frequency' for the category name, or treats the tally marks and the frequency total as the same thing
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate the roles in the activity: category = the group, tally = the marks you make, frequency = the count you end with
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child labels the category column 'frequency', or calls the marks the frequency

errorPatterns.pattern: Muddles 'label' and 'scale' — calls the category names the scale, or numbers an axis in uneven steps yet still calls it a scale
errorPatterns.nextMove: Define by use in the chart: the scale is the equal number steps up the axis; the labels say what each axis shows
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child places the 'scale' tag on the labels, or draws unequal number steps

responseLevels.gap: Misuses core terms in context — mislabels chart parts and cannot tell discrete from continuous
responseLevels.full: Uses the full data vocabulary accurately in the activity — labels title/axes/scale/categories, distinguishes tally and frequency, and justifies discrete vs continuous with the in-between test
responseLevels.partial: Uses the everyday terms (bar chart, tally, category) correctly while building, but muddles frequency vs tally or discrete vs continuous

assess.diagnosticPrompt: We counted how many pets each child has, and we also measured how tall everyone is. Set up a bar chart for the pet data and talk me through it as you go — and for each of the two things we collected, tell me whether it's discrete or continuous. (Listen for the terms USED correctly in the activity, not for definitions.)
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Using the words correctly WHILE building and describing the chart reveals real command; a child who has only memorised definitions mislabels the scale, calls the counts 'categories', or tags height 'discrete' because it's written as a whole number. Requiring use-in-action, not a definition, is what discriminates.
